1.open: Who is someone who taught you something you still use today, like a skill, a recipe or a habit?
questions: Paul calls Timothy "my beloved child" (v. 2) and says he remembers him "night and day in my prayers" (v. 3). What does it mean to you that someone might pray for you like that, or that you could pray for someone else that way?

Paul points to "your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (v. 5). Who passed faith, or something good, down to you? What did they actually do that made a difference?
Paul tells Timothy to "fan into flame the gift of God" (v. 6). When has your faith or your energy felt more like embers than a fire? What helps you stir it up again, and what makes it harder?
Verse 7 says, "God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control." What are you afraid of right now? How does this verse sit with you when you are honest about that fear?

Paul tells Timothy not to be "ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner" (v. 8). In Paul's day, being linked to a prisoner was risky. What might it cost someone today to stand beside a person others look down on?
Verse 9 says God saved us "not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us." How does that land when you feel you have to prove yourself, to God or to other people?

Paul says, "I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him" (v. 12). Scholars are not sure whether Paul means his life or the message he was given. Either way, what would it look like to trust God with something you cannot keep safe yourself? If trust feels hard right now, what makes it hard?

Paul says everyone in Asia "deserted" him, yet Onesiphorus "often refreshed me" and "searched diligently until he found me" (vv. 15-17). Who has been an Onesiphorus to you? Who might need you to be one for them?
1.life: Think of one person who has stood by you or taught you well. This week, write or call to thank them in specific words. If someone you know is feeling alone or looked down on, reach out and spend time with them.
1.prayer: Thank God for the people who handed faith down to you. Ask him to stir up what has gone cold and to replace fear with "power, love, and self-control." Pray by name for someone who feels deserted.
1.tip: Verse 7 can sting for people who live with anxiety, because it can sound like fear means something is wrong with their faith. Help the group hear it as encouragement, not a rebuke. Paul is writing to someone who was likely feeling timid, and he does not scold him. He reminds him what God has given. Let people name their fears without trying to fix them.

2.open: Who is someone who taught you something you still use today, and what did they teach you?
questions: Paul says, "be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus" (v. 1). Notice he does not say be strong in yourself. What difference does that make when you feel tired or worn down?

Paul asks Timothy to entrust what he has heard to "faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well" (v. 2). Who passed their faith on to you, and who might you be passing it to, even in small ways?
Paul uses a soldier, an athlete and a farmer (vv. 3-6). Which of the three pictures fits where you are right now, and why?
Paul is chained like a criminal, yet says, "the word of God cannot be chained!" (v. 9). What does it mean to you that the message keeps going even when people struggle or are held back?

Verses 11 to 13 end with, "if we are faithless, He remains faithful." Christians read the lines just before it differently: some hear a warning, others hear mainly reassurance. How do you hear these verses today?
Paul warns against "quarreling over words" and "empty chatter" (vv. 14, 16). How can we tell the difference between an argument that is worth having and one that only wears people down?
Paul says a servant of the Lord must be "kind to everyone" and "gently reprove those who oppose him" (vv. 24, 25). Where is it hardest for you to be gentle when you think someone is wrong?
Verse 15 speaks of being "an unashamed workman." If you feel unsure or doubtful about parts of the Bible, what would help you handle it honestly and keep learning?
2.life: Pick one person you could encourage in their faith this week, whether younger, older or the same age. Send them a note or invite them for coffee, and share one thing that has helped you keep going.
2.prayer: Ask God for strength "in the grace that is in Christ Jesus" for whatever you are facing this week. Pray for kindness and patience with people you disagree with.
2.tip: Verses 12 and 13 can stir up an argument about whether a believer can lose salvation. Say plainly that Christians differ, give each view one fair sentence, and bring the group back to the closing words that Christ "remains faithful."

3.open: Who is someone you learned a lot from growing up, and what did you pick up from them that wasn't in words?
questions: Paul says people will be "lovers of themselves, lovers of money" (v. 2). Which items on his list sound most like our world today, and which are easiest to miss in ourselves?

Verse 5 describes "having a form of godliness but denying its power." What might that look like in a church or a home, and how can someone tell the difference between the outward look and the real thing?

Verses 6 and 7 talk about people who are "always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth." Why can someone keep taking in ideas and still not arrive anywhere? Have you ever done that?

Paul reminds Timothy of his own teaching, conduct, purpose and faith, and of the sufferings he went through (vv. 10, 11). Why does Paul point to how he lived and not only to what he said? How much does it matter to you that a teacher's life matches their words?
Verse 12 says "all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted." What does opposition look like where you live, and what do you do when it is small and not dramatic?
Verse 14 says to "continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed." Who taught you what you know about God, good or bad, and what has stayed with you?

Paul says Scripture is "God-breathed" and useful for "instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (v. 16). Which of those four do you find hardest to welcome, and why? If you feel unsure or even doubtful about the Bible, what questions do you carry?
3.life: Pick one person who has shown you what living for Jesus looks like. This week, thank them in a note or a call, and name one thing you learned from watching them.
3.prayer: Ask God for wisdom to tell what is true from what only looks good. Pray for steady faith for anyone in the group who feels worn down, and thank God for the people who taught you.
3.tip: Verses 6 and 7 use belittling language about women, and it can sting or draw a quick defense. Name it calmly, note that readers differ on how much it reflects its time, and steer back to Paul's main concern: teachers who mislead and people who never settle on the truth. Also, Christians differ on what verses 16 and 17 say about Scripture and church tradition, so say so in one line and keep moving.

4.open: Who is someone who stuck with you through a hard season, and what did they do that you still remember?
questions: Paul tells Timothy to "Preach the word" and to be ready whether the moment is convenient or not (v. 2). Where do you find it hardest to speak up about your faith, or to speak the truth gently, when the timing feels wrong?
Paul warns that people will gather "teachers to suit their own desires" (v. 3). Why is it so easy to want only the teaching we already like? How can we tell when we are doing it?

In verse 7 Paul says, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." Notice he does not say he won every argument or never stumbled. What do you think finishing well looks like for an ordinary person?
Paul looks ahead to a reward for "all who crave His appearing" (v. 8). What do you honestly feel when you think about Jesus returning: longing, worry, curiosity, or not much at all?

Paul admits that Demas left "in his love of this world" (v. 10), and he asks for Mark, who is "useful to me in the ministry" (v. 11). Mark had once let Paul down. What does this say about second chances, and where have you given or received one?
Paul, in prison and near the end, still asks for his cloak and "my scrolls" (v. 13). What does that small request tell you about him, and about being honest regarding what we need?

At his first defense "no one stood with me," yet Paul prays, "May it not be charged against them" (v. 16). Then he says, "the Lord stood by me and strengthened me" (v. 17). Have you ever felt alone and still sensed help from somewhere? If not, what would you want God to be like in a moment like that?
Paul ends a heavy chapter with "Grace be with you all" (v. 22). How does grace change the way we think about finishing well, failing, or being let down by others?
4.life: Think of one person who is worn out, lonely or discouraged. This week, reach out in a way that costs you something small, like a visit, a call or a handwritten note, and tell them you are glad they are in your life.
4.prayer: Thank God that he stands with us even when people do not. Ask for strength to stay faithful in your own race, and for grace toward those who have let you down.
4.tip: Verses 14 and 15 sound harsh, and some people will stumble on Paul naming an enemy and saying the Lord will repay him. Point out that Paul leaves judgment to God and, in verse 16, asks that those who abandoned him not be blamed. It may also help to say briefly that Christians differ on whether Paul or a later follower wrote this letter, then return to the text in front of you.
